analytic.title: A Symbolic Schedulability Technique of Real-Time Systems Modeled by P-Time Petri Nets

div.p: This paper addresses the schedulability analysis of real-time systems modeled by P-Time Petri nets. The proposed approach is based on the consideration of the reachability graph of the (untimed) underlying Petri net of the studied model. The schedulability analysis is then conducted in two steps. Once a feasible firing sequence (called occurrence sequence) is highlighted, thanks to a firing instant based approach the timing constraints are added, yielding an inequality system representing its timing behavior. Thus, deciding whether a firing sequence is schedulable or not takes the form of the solution of a linear programming problem. Furthermore, the modification of a timing constraint does not alter the form of the obtained system, helping adjusting accurately timing properties in a specifications refinement purpose.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: A real-time system can be defined as a system whose correctness depends not only on the logical result of computations, but also on the time at which the results are produced. For this kind of systems, the response-time constraints must be imperatively respected and a missed deadline can generally lead to significant loss. Indeed, it must process information and produce its response within a specified time or it risks severe consequences, including system failure. For such systems the process of verifying whether a sequence of operations (or tasks) completes without violation of timing constraints is referred to as schedulability analysis.

Schedulability analysis can be thought of as, in many cases, the first step towards a control strategy as it ensures that a particular firing sequence of interest can occur without any violation of timing constraints.

Petri nets (PN) [5], [9] are recognized as an convenient tool for the modeling and the analysis of asynchronous, discrete event dynamic systems with concurrency. Proposed originally as a causal logic model explicitly neglecting time, they have been extended in order to meet the requirements of specific application areas. In particular for time dependent or real-time systems [1], [2], [12], [15], [16] PNs are extended with two time parameters representing a minimum and a maximum delay.

This interval of firability, for Merlin's model [8] also called Time Petri Nets (TPN), is associated with each transition of the model representing its static earliest and latest firing time. For the model considered in this paper, namely P-time Petri Nets (P-TPN) [6], the timing constraints are attached to places and its firing rule is based on three tokens states (unavailable, available and dead).

Many analysis techniques of time models are exhaustive simulation based approaches [1], [3], [11] aimed at generating the set of all reachable markings and cannot be used to determine the end-to-end delay in task execution which is a key requirement for real-time systems analysis.

Tsai et al. [12] address the problem of real-time specifications schedulability regarding a set of imposed timing constraints. Their approach uses a PN model called Timing Constraint Petri Nets (TCPN) which have a weak firing rule (i.e. transitions are not forced to fire). The authors proposed method relies on a three-steps analysis : specification modeling, reachability simulation and timing analysis. Although, TCPN possess a great expressive power, practicaly, it appears to be complicated to use. Inspired by the work of Tsai et al., Xu et al. [10] propose a compositional approach based on absolute and relative firing domains to reduce the complexity of schedulability analysis for time critical systems modeled by TPN. The authors proposed to separate timing properties from other behavioral properties. More recently, to overcome the state space explosion problem inherent to enumerative based techniques, Bernardi et al. [4] developed a structural performance analysis method for TPN. It uses linear programming techniques and is aimed at computing performance bounds to partially characterize the quantitative behavior of systems modeled by TPN by exploiting their structural properties. In [7] the authors solve some problems (reachability, bounded timing analysis . . . ) by investigating the reachability graph of the underlying untimed net of the time Petri net considered. They use linear programming techniques but their proposed method is restricted to a subclass of safe time Petri nets, namely, loop-closed Petri nets.

This paper introduces a new schedulability analysis technique for real-time systems. It uses P-Time Petri nets as a modeling tool and is based on the analysis of the set of feasible occurrence sequences of the underlying (untimed) PN of the P-TPN model considered. More precisely, the approach allows to check whether an occurrence sequence is schedulable in the associated P-TPN. The developed technique exploits the equivalence between a particular behavior of the modeled system and a linear inequality system. Unlike the aforementioned approaches, the presented method is neither restricted to subclasses of PN nor to safe models and the modification of the timing constraints does not alter the form of the obtained system (i.e. it is not necessary to restart the whole analysis process), helping adjusting accurately timing properties in a specifications refinement purpose. Furthermore, some decidability results about reachability for P-TPN are also presented.

The paper is organized as follows: a brief remainder of the basics of untimed Petri nets followed by a formal definition of P-Time Petri nets is realized in the next section. Section three deals with the schedulability analysis approach based on the firing instant notion. Section four discusses the reachability problem of P-TPN based on the reachability graph of the underlying (untimed) Petri net. A real-time manufacturing illustrative example is proposed in the fifth one.
Finally, in the last section some conclusions are presented.

div.head: II. PETRI NETS
div.p: A. Untimed Petri Nets [5], [9] A Place/Transition net (P/T net) is a structure N = (P, T, P re, P ost), where P is a set of m places; T is a set of n transitions. P re : P × T → N and P ost : P × T → N are the pre and post incidence functions that specify the arcs; C = P ost -P re is the incidence matrix. The preset and postset of a node X ∈ P ∪ T are denoted • X and X • . A marking is a vector M : P → N that assigns to each place of a P/T net a nonnegative integer number of tokens, represented by black dots. M (p) is the marking of place p. A net system N ; M 0 is a net N with an initial marking M 0 . A transition t is marking enabled at M if M ≥ P re(•, t). A transition t enabled at M may fire, yielding the marking M = M +C(•, t). A marking M is reachable in N ; M 0 iff there exists a firing sequence σ such that M 0 [σ > M . The set of all markings reachable from M 0 defines the reachability set of N ; M 0 and is denoted R(N ; M 0 ). Finally, we denote P R(N ; M 0 ) the potentially reachable set, i.e., the set of all markings M ∈ N m for which there exists a vector → y ∈ N n that satisfies the state equation
div.formula: M = M 0 + C. → y , i.e., P R(N ; M 0 ) = M ∈ N m |∃ → y ∈ N n : M = M 0 + C. → y .
div.p: It holds that R(N ; M 0 ) ⊆ P R(N ; M 0 ). A Petri net having no directed circuits is called acyclic.

div.head: IV. SCHEDULABILITY AND REACHABILITY
div.p: In a P-TPN the reachability of a particular marking M n can be discussed in terms of schedulability of a firing sequence σ ∈ L(M 0 , M n ). Indeed, marking M n will be reachable if a schedule starting from M 0 and leading to M n exists. In the presented approach determining whether M n is reachable may required the analysis of all the possible firing sequences from M 0 to M n for the untimed underlying PN of the P-TPN considered.
The following theorem can be stated. Theorem 1: A marking M n is unreachable in a P-TPN if it is unreachable in its associated underlying untimed PN (i.e. its UPN).

The proof is straightforward as the set of reachable markings of the P-TPN is a subset of the one obtained from its UPN. Indeed, due to the timing constraints, some feasible firing sequence of the UPN (i.e. element of L(M 0 )) can become infeasible on the associated P-TPN.
Theorem 2: It is decidable whether a marking M n in a P-TPN is reachable or not if L(M 0 , M n ) is a finite set.

Indeed, since L(M 0 , M n ) is a finite set, only a finite set of firing sequences which reach M n in the UPN exists. For each δ ∈ L(M 0 , M n ) it can be decided whether it is schedulable or not in the associated P-TPN. If it exists at least one schedulable firing sequence then M n is reachable in the P-TPN otherwise M n is not rechable according to Theorem 1 Theorem 3: [13] Let N be an acyclic Petri net. • A marking M n is reachable from M 0 if and only if there exists a non negative integer solution → σ satisfying the state equation M n = M 0 + C. → σ , i.e., R(N ; M 0 ) = P R(N ; M 0 ). Theorem 4: It is decidable whether a marking M n in a P-TPN is reachable or not if its underlying untimed PN is acyclic. The proof is straightforward with regard to theorem 3.

In [14] Ramachandran et al. proposed a net transformation procedure which convert a general Petri net into an acyclic one. Their basic idea is to expand the considered PN into multiple layers with the places of the n th layer forming the input for the (n + 1) th layer. Thanks to the developed approach, based on a net expansion scheme, the necessary and sufficient reachability condition stated for acyclic PN can be extended to any general Petri net.

Theorem 5: [14] In a general Petri net, a marking M n ∈ R(N ; M 0 ) if and only if there exists a positive integer α such that the state equation of the α-stage expanded Petri net M α,n = M α,0 + C α .y has a non-negative integer solution.

With M α,0 (resp. M α,n ) the initial (resp. the n th ) marking of the α-stage expanded Petri net and C α its incidence matrix. Intuitively, α can be seen as the net expansion factor and it represents the length of the firing sequences (i.e. the number of transitions) for which all the states can be fully obtained.
So, the following lemma can be straightforwardly stated. Lemma 1: It is decidable whether a marking M n in a P-TPN is reachable or not.
The proof relies on the previous theorem 5 (labeled theorem 4 in [14]).

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: Time represents a major issue in the analysis of real-time systems. Indeed, for such systems where all tasks are timeconstrained, this parameter does not affect only the system performances but also its correctness. Thus, an acceptable behavior depends not only on the order of the events but particularly on the time at which the results are produced.

In this paper, a new schedulability analysis technique for real-time systems modeled by P-time Petri net is presented. The adopted approach separates timing properties from behavioral ones and yields to a linear inequality system obtained for a feasible occurrence sequence of the untimed underlying PN. This system is written once and this can be done for symbolic values, as shown in the illustrative example case study. Indeed, the ability of not considering only numerical quantities is used in order to test and adjust the pre-defined real-time specifications. It allows the modification of the timing constraints without altering the form of the obtained system.
An issue currently being investigated is the determination of a compositional or modular scheme allowing to simplify a complex occurrence sequence into several subsequences ones.
